newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: Budget crisis at U.N. unabated without U.S. funds.
newsitem.headline: Budget crisis at U.N. unabated without U.S. funds.

text.p: Teetering on the verge of bankruptcy, the United Nations closes out 1996 with a budget shortfall of $2.3 billion, more than half of it owed by Washington, a senior U.N. official said on Thursday.

Joseph Connor, the U.N. undersecretary for management and administration, said year-end payments from members were disappointing, well below levels promised to the world body despite cuts in personnel and operating expenses.

"Uncertainty is mounting, we are doing something we should not be doing, we are borrowing long and we're running out of cash," said Connor, the former chief executive officer of the Price Waterhouse accounting firm.
"It can only be cured by payments by member states."
Most of the debt is owed for past peacekeeping operations, totalling $1.7 billion. In addition, $600 million is owed for dues that pay for the regular operating budget.

Washington did make a $150 million payment to the U.N. for monies owed for the regular budget on Dec. 2. However, the U.N. had forecast an additional $63 million in U.S. payments before the year's end, money that will not be seen now.
According to U.N. data, the United States owes 69 percent of the total budget shortfall in the regular budget and 54 percent for peacekeeping, or more than $1.3 billion in total.
Of the U.S. debt, $377 million was for regular budget and $926 million for peacekeeping, $693 million of that amount for past peacekeeping operations and $233 million for current.
Fresh payments from the United States cannot be made until 1997, at the earliest, as funds must be approved by the U.S. Congress which reconvenes after the new year.

Russia, the second highest debtor to the U.N., also fell short of expected payments. Connor said after a projected late December payment, Russia will have paid $305 million to both the regular budget and peacekeeping in 1996, down from $400 million pledged.
"It is not as much as they hoped to pay, but still it's a lot of cash," Connor said.
The Republican-dominated Congress unilaterally cut Washington's peacekeeping contribution and put conditions on payments during the 1996 congressional session.

An omnibus spending bill signed by President Bill Clinton in September said the U.N. had to fulfil two out of the three stipulations including cuts in personnel, a zero-growth budget and other requirements.

Connor said U.N. Secretary-General Boutros Boutros-Ghali was extremely concerned over not only the financial crisis, but "to what this continued situation means relative to actions of member states that consistently pay without condition."
Connor said valuable managerial staff talent and time was being wasted on the budgetary shortfall.
"Continuing financial crisis diverts attention and would negatively impact on efforts for internal reform and renewal of the Secretariat," Connor said.
As of Nov. 30, a total of 97 member states have paid their regular budget assessments in full, slightly better than the 90 states which did at the same time last year.
But Connor said the cash budget shortfall at the end this year showed "no significant improvement since last year and the substantial deterioration from 1994 and 1993."
